passage: The design office in Kochi was quiet at six, just Kavitha and Jomon finishing the brochure files. Kavitha had just shared the draft where she'd spelt the client's name wrong on the cover; she'd spotted it herself a minute too late. Then, from Jomon's desk, came a low, satisfied chortle. Heh-heh-heh. Kavitha's face went hot. He must have seen it. She typed and deleted a message twice. Finally she walked over, arms folded. "Go on, say it. The cover." Jomon looked up, confused. "What cover? The printer file finally exported without crashing. Four tries!" He turned his screen to show her. Kavitha let her arms drop. Then he opened the draft, saw the name, and chortled again, softer this time. "Okay, that one is funny. But I've done worse. Fix it, and let's go home."

qa.q: What had Kavitha spelt wrong on the cover?
qa.a: The client's name.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she heard Jomon chortle?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and defensive, her face going hot, because she assumed he was laughing at her mistake; it turned out he was relieved about the printer file.

qa.q: What went right when Kavitha walked over, and what could she keep doing?
qa.a: She asked instead of stewing over it, which revealed the real reason for the chortle; checking like that is better than guessing from a sound.

qa.q: How might Jomon's second chortle have felt different to Kavitha?
qa.a: It came softer and with "I've done worse", so it likely felt like shared humour rather than mocking.

grounding: Shows a quiet chortle read as mockery that was actually relief, and how shared humour differs from laughter at someone's mistake.

passage:
Dear Swati,
Something small has been bothering me, so I'm writing it down for you instead of saying it badly on the phone.
In Dr Pillai's seminar on Tuesday, I answered his question about the 1857 revolt with the wrong year. He sat back and gave this little chortle, lips closed, shoulders shaking, like he was enjoying a private joke. Two boys in the back smirked. I felt about six years old.
But yesterday I walked past his office and heard the same chortle while he was reading something on his own. He looked genuinely delighted. And later he told me he'd made the exact same mistake in his own viva, years ago.
So now I don't know. Was it at me, or was he remembering himself? Maybe both. I'm going to ask him, gently, at office hours. What would you do?
Love,
Ritu

qa.q: What did Ritu answer wrong in Dr Pillai's seminar?
qa.a: The year of the 1857 revolt.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Dr Pillai chortled in the seminar?
qa.a: Ritu felt small and humiliated, "about six years old", especially with the smirks; now Ritu is unsure whether the chortle was mocking or a private memory.

qa.q: What small step is Ritu planning, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Asking Dr Pillai gently at office hours, because the same chortle has shown up in different contexts and only he can say what he meant.

qa.q: What might Dr Pillai have been thinking when he chortled?
qa.a: He may have been amused remembering his own identical viva mistake, not mocking Ritu, though the smirking boys made it land badly.

grounding: Shows how the same chortle can signal private amusement or feel mocking, depending on context.

passage: You want the roommate story, Thomas? Fine. It's me, Leela, confessing on your podcast. My first month in the hostel, my roommate Farzana would sit on her bed with her phone and chortle. Not laugh, chortle. A low, smug little gurgle. Every night. And I was convinced she was reading the class group chat and laughing at my messages. I'd asked a silly question there, you see. I stopped talking to her. Two weeks of silence. Then one night she chortled and just held the phone out. It was a video of a cat falling into a fish tank. I laughed so hard I choked. She said, "I've been dying to show you these, but you always looked angry." We've been sending each other cat videos ever since. That little chortle? Now it just means she's found a good one.

qa.q: What was in the video Farzana held out?
qa.a: A cat falling into a fish tank.

qa.q: What was Leela worried about during those two weeks?
qa.a: Leela was worried and hurt, convinced Farzana was mocking a silly question in the class group chat; the chortle was really private amusement.

qa.q: What could Leela have done earlier instead of going silent?
qa.a: Asked Farzana what was so funny, which would have cleared up the chortle and saved two weeks of silence.

qa.q: How did Farzana see those two weeks?
qa.a: Farzana wanted to share the videos but thought Leela always looked angry, so she held back too.

grounding: Shows a chortle at private amusement misread as mockery, and how sharing the joke turned it into bonding.

passage:
Team lead's note, customer support team, Friday.
This week I noticed a pattern with Joseph, our newest team member. When I gave him feedback in the team chat about a late ticket, he replied, "haha ok lol 😅". When Rhea corrected his reply template, he wrote, "lol my bad 😂". At first I read it as not taking things seriously. Then on Thursday I saw his face after one of those messages: he wasn't smiling at all. So I asked him to have tea. I told him the lols were fine, but I wondered how the feedback actually felt. He said it embarrassed him, and "lol" felt safer than admitting that. I said I'd give feedback privately from now on, and that he could just write "noted" if he preferred. On Friday his message to Rhea was "Noted, thanks, fixing now 👍". I'll keep checking in.
— Zubin

qa.q: How did Joseph reply to the feedback about the late ticket?
qa.a: He replied, "haha ok lol 😅".

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he typed "lol" after feedback?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, and the "lol" softened that; Zubin first read it as not taking things seriously, which shows the same letters can hide discomfort.

qa.q: What did Zubin try that helped?
qa.a: He noticed Joseph's face, asked privately over tea how the feedback felt, and moved feedback out of the group chat.

qa.q: How did Zubin's reading of the lols change after seeing Joseph's face?
qa.a: At first Zubin thought Joseph was being casual about mistakes; after seeing he wasn't smiling, Zubin saw the lols as a cover for discomfort.

grounding: Shows a young adult using lol and laughing emojis to soften uncomfortable feedback, and a lead learning that tone and context matter more than the letters.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Had to tell Jagdish I can't make his cousin's wedding. I typed, "Bro I'm so sorry, can't come, exam on Monday lol 😅". I added the lol so it wouldn't sound heavy. Then I stared at it. Does lol make it sound like I don't care? Like his cousin's wedding is a joke? I almost deleted it.
He replied after twenty minutes: "lol ok".
Now I'm lying here reading those two words. Jagdish uses lol for everything, even "my phone died lol". So maybe it's fine. Or maybe it's the flat lol, the one that means he's annoyed and doesn't want to say.
I called him. He picked up laughing about something else, then said, "Obviously I'm a bit sad, but exams are exams." We talked for ten minutes. That lol was half and half, I think.
— Manoj

qa.q: Why couldn't Manoj go to the wedding?
qa.a: Because of an exam on Monday.

qa.q: What was Manoj worried about after sending the message?
qa.a: Manoj was anxious that the lol made it sound careless about the wedding, and later that Jagdish's flat "lol ok" meant he was annoyed.

qa.q: Which choice helped Manoj, and why?
qa.a: Calling Jagdish instead of reading the two words over and over, because hearing his voice showed he was a bit sad but not angry.

qa.q: How did Jagdish seem to feel about Manoj missing the wedding?
qa.a: He was a bit sad but understanding, saying "exams are exams", so the lol carried some disappointment and some acceptance.

grounding: Shows a young adult using lol to soften a message and learning that the same lol can mean humour, politeness or discomfort.

subtype: Types of laughter and social bonding [Expressing]
passage: On her first day at the insurance office in Guwahati, Zeenat nearly dropped her tea when a huge guffaw exploded from the canteen corner. It was Bhupen from claims, head thrown back, slapping the table at a joke only he seemed to find that funny. A few people rolled their eyes. Zeenat, who had grown up in a quiet household where laughter stayed small, stiffened a little. By the second week, though, she noticed something. When the printer jammed and everyone groaned, Bhupen's belly laugh made them all laugh too, even the grumpy manager. On Friday, when Zeenat told a story about a goat blocking her bus, Bhupen laughed so loudly and so genuinely that she started laughing too, properly, from her stomach. Later she realised it was the first time anyone at work had laughed with her, not near her.

qa.q: What did Zeenat tell a story about on Friday?
qa.a: A goat blocking her bus.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel when she first heard Bhupen's guffaw?
qa.a: She was startled and a little uncomfortable, since laughter stayed small in her quiet household; by Friday she felt included when he laughed at her story.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who finds a colleague's loud laugh jarring?
qa.a: Watch for a while, as Zeenat did, since the laugh may be warm and bring people together even if the style feels bold at first.

qa.q: How do the people who rolled their eyes seem to see Bhupen's laugh?
qa.a: They seem to find it too much, which shows the same guffaw can feel bold to some and warm to others.

grounding: Shows a young adult's loud guffaws and belly laughs building closeness at work while feeling bold to someone from a quieter background.

passage:
"Chinmay, you did it again," Santosh said as they walked out of the comedy night.
"Did what?"
"The cackle. The one where you sound like a villain in a cartoon. The whole back row turned round."
Chinmay laughed. "I can't help it! The mango-seller joke got me."
"I know. Honestly, it made the comic laugh too."
"Wait, really?"
"Did you not see? He stopped and pointed at you. 'That guy gets it.'"
Chinmay grinned. "My Nani laughs exactly like that. At home, nobody even notices."
"At my place we chuckle. Quietly. If my uncle laughed like you, Mummy would ask if he's feeling okay."
They both laughed, Santosh with a low chuckle, Chinmay with a short, loud burst he tried to swallow.
"Next time," Santosh said, "sit closer to the front. Then only the comic gets the cackle."

qa.q: Which joke made Chinmay cackle?
qa.a: The mango-seller joke.

qa.q: How does Chinmay feel when Santosh says the comic pointed at him?
qa.a: He seems surprised and pleased, grinning; he also seems a little self-conscious, since he tries to swallow his next laugh.

qa.q: What does Santosh suggest, and why is it a friendly idea?
qa.a: Sitting closer to the front, so Chinmay can laugh freely without bothering the back row, instead of asking him to stop laughing.

qa.q: How might Santosh's family see Chinmay's cackle?
qa.a: In a family where people chuckle quietly, it might seem odd or even worrying, while at Chinmay's home it is normal.

grounding: Shows friends with different laughs, a cackle and a chuckle, finding that shared laughter bonds them while the style feels bold in one home and normal in another.

subtype: Types of laughter and social bonding [Expressing]
passage: The night I remember best from that first year is the power cut. It was August, the hostel was dark and sticky, and Ankita and I were stuck on the terrace with one candle and a packet of biscuits. I'm Raghav, by the way, and back then I laughed politely, a little chuckle, nothing more. Ankita tried to tell a ghost story and knocked the candle over into the biscuit packet. I don't know what happened to me. I laughed from somewhere deep, a real belly laugh, bent double, tears on my face. She started too, a loud snort that made me laugh even harder. We couldn't stop for five minutes. The lights came back and we were still gasping. After that night we were different: we'd look at each other in lectures and just grin. I think that laugh was when we became real friends.

qa.q: What did Ankita knock over?
qa.a: The candle, into the biscuit packet.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling during the belly laugh on the terrace?
qa.a: Raghav felt pure, uncontrolled joy, bent double with tears; it was surprising too, since Raghav usually only chuckled politely.

qa.q: What does the story suggest about building a close friendship?
qa.a: Moments of shared, spontaneous laughter can bring people closer than polite chuckles; letting the guard down helped.

qa.q: How did the laughter seem to change things for Ankita?
qa.a: After that night she would grin at Raghav in lectures, which suggests she felt closer and more at ease too.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from polite chuckles to a shared belly laugh that builds closeness.

passage: The results list went up outside the Kalimpong college office at noon. Ganga found her roll number, then found the red mark beside it: one paper failed. She walked calmly to the bus stop, sat down on the bench, and her eyes filled before she could stop them. She kept wiping them angrily with her sleeve. Dolma, her classmate from the next village, sat down beside her and said nothing for a while. "I'm so stupid, crying in public," Ganga muttered. "Crying isn't stupid," Dolma said. "You've barely slept since March." Ganga cried properly then, and after a few minutes her shoulders dropped. Dolma bought two cups of tea from the stall. "Tonight, sleep. Tomorrow, we'll go and ask about the supplementary exam together." Ganga nodded, wiping her face. "And if you feel this low every day," Dolma added, "we tell Ma'am at the counselling cell."

qa.q: How many papers did Ganga fail?
qa.a: One paper.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she wiped her eyes angrily?
qa.a: She was upset and ashamed of crying in public, calling herself stupid; the tears were also a release of weeks of stress and little sleep.

qa.q: What wise steps did Dolma suggest?
qa.a: Sleep tonight, ask about the supplementary exam together tomorrow, and talk to the counselling cell if Ganga feels that low every day.

qa.q: How did Dolma see Ganga's crying?
qa.a: Dolma saw it as a natural release after months of little sleep, not weakness, and stayed with her calmly.

grounding: Shows a young adult crying under exam stress, the tears easing tension, and a friend suggesting rest, support and counselling if it continues.

passage: Thabo's twelve-hour shift at the Johannesburg hospital ended at seven. In the staff room he sat down to change his shoes and suddenly couldn't. His hands stopped, his throat closed, and he was crying, quietly, head down, for the third time that week. He felt ashamed. Nurses don't do this, he told himself. Zeynep, a nurse from the next ward, came in for her bag and stopped. She sat on the bench, not too close. "Long one?" He nodded. "I keep crying after shifts. I'm fine, I'm just tired." "Tired is real," Zeynep said. "And three times in a week is your body telling you something. The staff wellness counsellor sees people the same day. I went last year." Thabo looked up. "You?" "Me. It helped." She wrote the extension on his hand. He called it before he went home.

qa.q: How long was Thabo's shift?
qa.a: Twelve hours.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling while crying in the staff room?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and ashamed, telling himself nurses don't do this; the crying three times in one week also suggests he was worn out.

qa.q: What did Zeynep do that helped Thabo take the next step?
qa.a: She sat with him, took his tears seriously, shared that she had seen the counsellor herself, and gave him the extension.

qa.q: How did Zeynep read Thabo's tears differently from how he read them?
qa.a: Thabo saw them as weakness; Zeynep saw them as a sign of real tiredness that deserved support.

grounding: Shows a young adult crying from work burnout and a colleague encouraging rest and counselling when crying keeps happening.

passage: It had been three weeks since the breakup, and Shalini, Jahnavi's roommate in the girls' hostel, had heard her crying most nights. Tonight it was over a dropped plate in the mess. Jahnavi stood at the sink, tears running, hands shaking. "It's a plate," she laughed, crying harder. Shalini guided her back to the room and sat with her. "You're allowed to cry. But it's every night now. How are you sleeping?" "Badly. And I can't focus in class." Shalini listened for a long time. Then she said, "The college counsellor has evening hours till eight. It's seven now. Shall I walk with you?" Jahnavi hesitated. "What if they think I'm being dramatic?" "They won't. And I'll wait outside." Jahnavi washed her face. They walked there together, and Shalini sat on the bench outside until the door opened again.

qa.q: How long had it been since the breakup?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi worried about before seeing the counsellor?
qa.a: She was anxious that the counsellor would think she was being dramatic; underneath, she was exhausted and sad from weeks of crying.

qa.q: What did Shalini do that made the next step easier?
qa.a: She said crying was allowed, listened, noticed the pattern, and offered to walk Jahnavi to the counsellor that same evening and wait outside.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini had only said "It's just a plate"?
qa.a: Jahnavi might have felt dismissed and kept crying alone each night without reaching the counsellor.

grounding: Shows a young adult crying often after a breakup and a friend treating tears as valid while helping her reach counselling when it keeps happening.

passage: At his sister Radha's bidaai in the village of Kheda, Madhav stood by the decorated jeep and wept openly, big tears rolling into his moustache. Baljeet, his college friend visiting from Ludhiana, didn't know where to look. At home, men in his family went quiet at weddings, not teary. Was Madhav sad about losing his sister? Or angry about something? The women around them were crying too, and laughing, and singing all at once. Radha hugged Madhav, crying and smiling. When the jeep pulled away, Madhav wiped his face, grinning. Baljeet put a hand on his shoulder, unsure. "You okay?" Madhav laughed. "Okay? I'm the happiest I've been all year. She's marrying the man she chose. And I'll miss her every day." Baljeet nodded slowly. "Both, then." "Always both," Madhav said.

qa.q: Where did Radha's bidaai take place?
qa.a: In the village of Kheda.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling as he wept by the jeep?
qa.a: He felt both happy and sad at once: joy that Radha married the man she chose, and grief that he would miss her every day.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do that respected Madhav's own meaning?
qa.a: He asked "You okay?" instead of assuming, and accepted Madhav's answer that the tears were both joy and loss.

qa.q: How did Baljeet's own background shape how he read the tears?
qa.a: In Baljeet's family men go quiet at weddings, so he first wondered if Madhav was sad or angry, not that he could be joyful.

grounding: Shows a young adult weeping at a wedding farewell with mixed grief and joy, and a friend from a different background learning to ask what the tears mean.

passage: At the university graduation in Osaka, Kaito walked across the stage, bowed, took his certificate, and burst into tears on the way down the steps. Tuan, his flatmate from Hanoi, was waiting with flowers. He froze. Kaito had been so private all year; Tuan had never even seen him frown. Was something wrong? Had he got bad news? Around them, most graduates were smiling politely, a few crying behind their hands. Tuan stepped forward and held out the flowers carefully. "Kaito? Are you... okay?" Kaito laughed through his tears and wiped them hard with his sleeve. "My grandfather wanted to see this. He died in spring." Tuan's face fell. "I'm sorry." "No, no," Kaito said. "I'm happy. I'm sad. It's both. He would be proud." Tuan nodded and stood beside him quietly, flowers in hand, until Kaito was ready to go.

qa.q: Where was the university graduation?
qa.a: In Osaka.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling as he came down the steps crying?
qa.a: He felt grief for his grandfather who had died in spring, mixed with pride and happiness at graduating; he said himself it was both.

qa.q: What was wise about how Tuan responded?
qa.a: He asked gently instead of assuming, and then simply stayed beside Kaito, letting him set the meaning and the pace.

qa.q: What would change if Tuan had assumed the tears meant bad news?
qa.a: He might have rushed to fix something or looked for the problem, missing that Kaito was also proud and happy.

grounding: Shows a young adult weeping at graduation with grief and joy mixed, and a friend respecting the person's own meaning.

passage: On the last night in the college hostel, the girls' wing held a farewell in the common room. Madhuri, who was leaving for a job in Bengaluru, stood up to say goodbye and started weeping before she got past the first line. Gurpreet sat stiffly in the second row. In her family, even at funerals, people cried in their rooms, not in front of others. She wanted to go and hug Madhuri but felt it might embarrass her. Others were already crying and laughing and clapping. After the speeches, Gurpreet found Madhuri in the corridor. "Are these sad tears? Should I leave you alone?" Madhuri shook her head, still sniffling, and smiled. "Happy ones, mostly. Relief too. Four years, done! I'm going to miss all of you, but I made it." Gurpreet laughed and hugged her tight.

qa.q: Where was Madhuri leaving for?
qa.a: A job in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as Madhuri wept during her goodbye?
qa.a: She felt awkward and unsure, wanting to hug Madhuri but worried it might embarrass her, because in her family tears stay private.

qa.q: What small step helped Gurpreet support Madhuri?
qa.a: She found Madhuri privately and asked what kind of tears they were and whether to leave her alone.

qa.q: How did Madhuri see her own tears?
qa.a: She saw them as mostly happy and relieved after four years, with some sadness about missing her friends.

grounding: Shows a young adult weeping at a farewell in joy and relief, and a friend from a more private tradition asking before comforting.

passage: At the Navratri music programme in the Kotdwar temple courtyard, the older singers sat cross-legged on a durrie, singing a slow bhajan. When they finished, Jagdish, just back from college in Delhi, put two fingers in his mouth and let out a huge whistle and a whoop. "Woo! Encore!" A dozen heads turned. The old harmonium player blinked. The women near the front pressed their palms together politely, and a few people clapped softly. Jagdish's sister Ankita tugged his sleeve, her face red. "Bhaiya, it's a bhajan, not a rock show." Jagdish's grin faded. At his college fest, a whoop meant respect. He looked at the harmonium player again, who was smiling now, maybe amused, maybe not. For the next song, Jagdish folded his hands with everyone else, then clapped. At the end he walked up to the singers and thanked them properly.

qa.q: Where did the music programme take place?
qa.a: In the Kotdwar temple courtyard.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she tugged Jagdish's sleeve?
qa.a: She was embarrassed, her face red, because the whoop felt out of place at a bhajan; she may also have worried the singers were offended.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do next that showed respect?
qa.a: He followed the local way for the next song, folding his hands and clapping, then thanked the singers in person.

qa.q: How might the harmonium player have seen the whoop?
qa.a: He blinked and then smiled, so he may have been startled, or amused, or a bit put off; his face left it unclear.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding that whooping, welcome at a college fest, feels odd at a temple music programme, and adjusting to the venue.

passage: At Wanjiru's graduation in a stone hall in Edinburgh, the ceremony was hushed. Names were read, polite applause rippled, and people clapped with their hands low. Then the announcer read "Wanjiru Kamau", and Zanele, her friend from Johannesburg, leapt to her feet and ululated, a loud, joyful trill, followed by a whoop. The whole row stared. An elderly man in front turned round, frowning. Zanele sat down, cheeks warm but grinning. On stage, Wanjiru was laughing, one hand over her heart. Afterwards, outside, the elderly man approached them. "Sorry if I seemed rude," he said. "I've just never heard that at a graduation." "At home, if nobody does that, it's like your family didn't come," Zanele explained. He smiled. "Then I'm glad someone came." Wanjiru hugged Zanele. "Best sound in the hall."

qa.q: Where was Wanjiru's graduation?
qa.a: In a stone hall in Edinburgh.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling after she sat down?
qa.a: She felt a bit self-conscious, cheeks warm, but also proud and happy, still grinning after cheering for Wanjiru.

qa.q: What helped clear up the moment after the ceremony?
qa.a: The elderly man came to explain his frown, and Zanele explained what the cheering means at home, so both understood each other.

qa.q: What was it like for Wanjiru to hear the whoop?
qa.a: It made her laugh with her hand on her heart, and she later called it the best sound in the hall, so it felt like being celebrated.

grounding: Shows a young adult's joyful whooping at a graduation being welcome in one culture and odd in another, and how talking it through builds respect.

passage: At the college convocation in Jaipur, the announcer asked everyone to hold applause until the end of each department's list. Ritu had already practised her loudest whoop for Pooja's name. When "Pooja Meena, first rank" was read, Ritu's mouth opened, then she remembered. She clenched her fists and bounced on her seat instead, silently. A boy three seats down did whoop, loud and long, for his own friend. The announcer paused, and a teacher on stage frowned. Ritu winced for him. When the department list ended, the hall broke into clapping, and Ritu finally let out one big "Yes, Pooja!" along with everyone else's cheers. Pooja spotted her from the stage and waved. After the ceremony, Pooja teased, "I heard you. Nicely timed." Ritu grinned. "Took all my self-control."

qa.q: When did the announcer ask everyone to applaud?
qa.a: At the end of each department's list.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when Pooja's name was read?
qa.a: Ritu was bursting with excitement and pride for Pooja, clenching her fists to hold back the whoop she had practised.

qa.q: What worked about Ritu's choice to wait?
qa.a: Cheering when the list ended let her celebrate loudly without disrupting the ceremony, unlike the boy whose whoop made the announcer pause.

qa.q: How did the teacher on stage seem to see the early whoop?
qa.a: The teacher frowned, suggesting it felt disruptive in a hall where applause had been asked to wait.

grounding: Shows a young adult matching the timing and volume of cheering to the venue's norms as a form of respect.

subtype: Yelling at work or home and de-escalation [Regulating]
passage: In his uncle's hardware shop in Rewari, Eshaan was counting boxes of screws when Kiran, the older shop assistant, suddenly shouted at him. "You gave away the last pipe fittings without writing them down! Again!" A customer looked up. Eshaan felt his face go hot and his fists close. He wanted to shout back. Instead he breathed out slowly and lowered his voice. "Kiran bhaiya, I hear you're angry. I don't want to argue in front of customers. Can we check the book together after closing?" Kiran was still breathing hard, but he stopped. "After closing, then." At eight, they sat with the stock register. Eshaan had written the fittings down, just on the wrong page. Kiran rubbed his neck. "I shouted too fast. Sorry." Eshaan nodded. "Next time, can we just talk first?"

qa.q: Where did Eshaan and Kiran work?
qa.a: In his uncle's hardware shop in Rewari.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when Kiran shouted?
qa.a: He felt angry and embarrassed, his face going hot and his fists closing, and he wanted to shout back.

subtype: Yelling at work or home and de-escalation [Regulating]
passage: Chen and Nour had been sharing a flat in Toronto for a year. That Sunday, Nour came home to the sink full of dishes and snapped. "I'm always the one cleaning! Always!" Her voice filled the kitchen. Chen felt his chest tighten. Part of him wanted to shout back about the bins he always took out. He didn't. He set his mug down slowly and spoke quietly. "You're really upset. I want to hear it, but not like this. Can we talk in an hour?" Nour stopped, breathing hard, and nodded stiffly. An hour later she knocked on his door. "Sorry. I had a horrible shift, and the dishes were the last straw. Shouting isn't okay." Chen said, "Thanks. And you're right about the dishes." They made a chore chart on the fridge. Chen wrote his name next to Monday.

qa.q: How long had Chen and Nour shared the flat?
qa.a: For a year.

qa.q: What was Chen feeling when Nour snapped about the dishes?
qa.a: He felt tense and defensive, his chest tightening, and part of him wanted to shout back about the bins.

qa.q: Which choice helped Chen and Nour sort it out?
qa.a: Chen kept his voice low and asked to talk in an hour, which gave Nour time to cool down and apologise.

qa.q: How did Nour see her shouting afterwards?
qa.a: Nour admitted it came from a horrible shift and said shouting isn't okay, so she saw it as a slip she regretted.

grounding: Shows a young adult responding to a raised voice at home by staying calm, lowering their tone and asking to continue later.

subtype: Yelling at work or home and de-escalation [Regulating]
passage: It was the third time that week Sonali, the floor manager, had yelled at Nikita in the small meeting room of the Noida office. Today it was about a report Nikita hadn't even been assigned. Sonali slammed her palm on the table. "Are you stupid?" Nikita's hands were shaking. She kept her voice low and steady. "I can see you're upset. I'm not able to talk when I'm being shouted at. Can we continue later, with Anand from HR?" Sonali shouted louder. "Sit down!" Nikita stood up. "I'm going to step out now." She left the room, walked straight to the HR desk and told Anand what had happened, including the other two times. Anand listened, wrote it down, and said, "Thank you for telling me today. I'll speak to Sonali's manager this afternoon, and you won't be in a meeting alone with her until we've sorted this."

qa.q: What did Sonali slam on the table?
qa.a: Her palm.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: She was frightened, her hands shaking, but determined to stay calm and not accept being shouted at.

qa.q: Why was leaving and going to HR the right step?
qa.a: Sonali kept shouting after Nikita asked to continue later, and it was the third time that week, so getting support from HR was safer than staying.

qa.q: How did Anand respond when Nikita reported the shouting?
qa.a: Anand listened, wrote it down, thanked Nikita, promised to speak to Sonali's manager that afternoon, and made sure Nikita wouldn't be alone with her.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying calm and asking to continue later when yelled at, then leaving and getting support when the shouting continues.

subtype: Sighing to hide or show stress [Regulating]
passage: I still think about the group project in second year. I'm Chinmay, and I was the one with the loud sighs. Every time Kishore suggested something in our meetings, I'd let out a long, heavy breath, eyes on the ceiling. I told myself it was just tiredness. One day Kishore stopped mid-sentence and said quietly, "If my ideas are that bad, just say it." Everyone went silent. I realised how it had sounded: like I was sighing at him, not at the deadline. I apologised, awkwardly. After that I noticed the difference between two kinds of sighs. The slow, quiet one I took before a presentation actually helped me; it steadied my hands. The loud one in meetings only made people feel small. Now, if I need a sigh, I take the quiet kind, and I try to say what's really bothering me.

qa.q: What did Kishore say when he stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: "If my ideas are that bad, just say it."

qa.q: How did Kishore feel about Chinmay's sighs?
qa.a: Kishore felt hurt and dismissed, taking the sighs as a sign that his ideas were bad.

qa.q: What did Chinmay change after that meeting?
qa.a: Chinmay kept the slow, quiet sigh for calming nerves before presentations and tried to say what was really bothering him instead of sighing loudly at people.

qa.q: What would change if Chinmay had never noticed how the sighs sounded?
qa.a: Kishore might have stopped sharing ideas, and the group would have felt tense without knowing why.

grounding: Shows the difference between a slow sigh that steadies nerves and a loud sigh that feels dismissive, and a young adult becoming aware of their audience.

passage:
Coach's note, university badminton club, Thursday practice.
Binita has a good habit I want the others to copy: before every serve in a tight game, she takes one slow sigh through her mouth, shoulders dropping. Her serve is steadier after it. Today, though, I noticed another kind of sigh. When her doubles partner, Priya, missed an easy return, Binita let out a loud, sharp huff and turned away. Priya's face fell, and she missed the next two shots as well. After the session I spoke to Binita privately. I told her the slow sigh before serving was excellent and that the loud one probably felt like a verdict to her partner. She said she hadn't realised it was so loud, that she was frustrated with herself as much as with Priya. We agreed she will try a quiet exhale instead and say "next one" to Priya. I'll watch at Saturday's match.
— Coach Kiran

qa.q: What does Binita do before every serve in a tight game?
qa.a: She takes one slow sigh through her mouth, shoulders dropping.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she let out the loud huff?
qa.a: She was frustrated, partly with Priya's miss and partly with herself, as she later told the coach.

qa.q: What plan did the coach and Binita agree on?
qa.a: Binita will use a quiet exhale instead of a loud huff and say "next one" to Priya after a miss.

qa.q: How did Priya seem to experience Binita's loud sigh?
qa.a: Her face fell and she missed the next two shots, suggesting she felt judged and lost confidence.

grounding: Shows a young adult using a slow sigh to steady nerves and learning that a loud sigh at a teammate can feel dismissive.

subtype: Sighing to hide or show stress [Regulating]
passage:
Wednesday.
Big client call at 11. Before it, I sat in the washroom and did the slow sighs the yoga aunty taught Mummy and me: long breath in, longer sigh out, three times. It worked. My voice didn't shake once during the demo.
Then, at 3, Mohit asked for the third time how to export the report. And I sighed. Loudly. The whole desk heard it. He went red and said, "Never mind, I'll figure it out." I felt terrible. The same thing that saved me at 11 made him feel like a nuisance at 3.
I went over at 4 with two cups of chai and showed him properly. I said, "Sorry about the sigh, that was about my day, not you." He laughed a bit and said he'd write the steps down this time.
Note to self: sighs for me, quietly. Not at people.
— Aditi

qa.q: When was the big client call?
qa.a: At 11.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel after sighing loudly at Mohit?
qa.a: Aditi felt terrible and guilty on seeing Mohit go red and hearing him say he'd figure it out alone.

qa.q: What did Aditi do to repair things with Mohit?
qa.a: Aditi went over with chai, showed him the export properly, and apologised, explaining the sigh was about the day, not him.

qa.q: How did Mohit seem to take the loud sigh?
qa.a: He went red and backed off, which suggests he felt embarrassed and like a nuisance for asking again.

grounding: Shows a young adult using slow sighs to steady nerves and noticing that an audible sigh at a colleague feels dismissive.

passage:
Friday, 8 p.m.
I always hum on the walk home from the bus stop. Old film songs, badly. It's the one part of the day that's just mine.
Today, at the corner near the paan shop, a man on a scooter slowed down and gave a long whistle, looking right at me. Then another one. My humming stopped in my throat. I kept walking faster, didn't look at him. He laughed and rode off.
I called Bhupen from the next lane, because he'd told me to call anytime. He stayed on the phone till I reached my building. When I got home I told Mummy, and she said, "Beti, we'll tell the RWA secretary tomorrow and ask about the streetlight at that corner." She also saved the number for the women's helpline in my phone.
Funny how it's the same sound, whistling. When Bhupen whistles on the terrace, it's happy. That one wasn't.
— Nikita

qa.q: Where did the man on the scooter whistle at Nikita?
qa.a: At the corner near the paan shop.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when the man whistled?
qa.a: She felt scared and unsettled; her humming stopped in her throat and she walked faster without looking at him.

qa.q: What steps did Nikita and her mother take after the whistling?
qa.a: Nikita called Bhupen to stay on the phone, told Mummy, who planned to tell the RWA secretary and ask about the streetlight, and saved the helpline number.

qa.q: How is Bhupen's whistling different from the man's?
qa.a: Bhupen whistles on the terrace because he is happy; the man whistled at Nikita as a stranger on the street, which made her feel unsafe.

grounding: Shows humming and whistling as calm or joyful sounds, and a whistle aimed at a person in public as unwelcome harassment that she leaves and reports.

passage: Tanvir always whistled while he worked the pump in his family's field near Barabanki; it kept the rhythm of the long afternoons. His friend Tushar whistled too, but differently. Every evening when the college bus dropped the girls from the next village at the crossing, Tushar leaned on his cycle and whistled long, loud notes at them, grinning. Tanvir used to laugh along. This evening he noticed one of the girls, Shabnam, walk faster, clutching her bag, eyes on the ground. Her friend pulled her closer. Tanvir's stomach tightened. "Stop it," he said to Tushar. "They're scared." "It's just a whistle, yaar." "Not to them." Tushar rolled his eyes. The next day, the girls' teacher came with the pradhan and spoke to both boys' fathers. Tushar sulked. Tanvir admitted he'd laughed along and said sorry. That evening he kept whistling at the pump, and nowhere near the crossing.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir whistle while he worked?
qa.a: At the pump in his family's field near Barabanki.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he saw Shabnam walk faster?

qa.q: What did Tanvir do once he saw it was wrong?
qa.a: He told Tushar to stop, and when the teacher and pradhan came, he admitted he had laughed along and apologised.

qa.a: They seemed scared, walking faster and pulling close, so for them it was harassment, not fun.

grounding: Shows whistling as calm work rhythm in one setting and as unwelcome harassment when aimed at girls in public, and recognising the difference.

passage: Hafsa called her friend Sunaina from the post office phone booth in Bhadrak, bursting with news. "I got the teaching job in Cuttack! Starting June!" "Mm-hmm," Sunaina said. Hafsa frowned. She told her about the school, the hostel, the salary. "Mm-hmm. Mm." Flat, far away. Hafsa's excitement drained. Was Sunaina jealous? Or did she think Cuttack was a bad idea? Or was she just busy? She could hear clattering in the background. Hafsa took a breath. "Sunaina, you sound far away. Is this a bad time?" There was a pause, then a laugh. "Sorry! The dal is boiling over and Ammi's shouting. I heard 'job' and 'Cuttack' and nothing else. Tell me again in five minutes?" Hafsa laughed too. When Sunaina called back, her "mm-hmms" came quick and warm, with "and then?" after each one.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa get the teaching job?
qa.a: In Cuttack.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when Sunaina kept saying a flat "mm-hmm"?
qa.a: Her excitement drained and she felt hurt and unsure, wondering whether Sunaina was jealous, disapproving or just busy.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do instead of assuming?
qa.a: She named what she heard, that Sunaina sounded far away, and asked if it was a bad time.

qa.q: How did Sunaina's "mm-hmms" change once she called back?
qa.a: They came quick and warm, with "and then?" after each one, showing she was now really listening.

grounding: Shows a young adult hearing a flat mm-hmm on a call as possible distraction and checking rather than assuming.

passage: Mei was on a video call from her flat in Singapore with Nadia in Kuala Lumpur, explaining her plan to leave her engineering course and study design. Nadia listened, chin in hand. "Mm-hmm... mm-hmm." Then Mei described quitting before the exams. Nadia's sound changed: a long, low "Hmmm." Her eyebrows went up. Mei stopped. "That hmm. Is that a no?" Nadia smiled slightly. "It's a thinking hmm. Maybe a slight worried hmm. Why before the exams, not after?" Mei bit her lip. She had been hoping Nadia would just say yes. But the question was fair. "I guess... because I'm scared I'll lose my nerve." "That's a real reason," Nadia said. "Just check it's the only one." They talked for another hour. Mei ended the call with two lists on her notepad and a clearer head.

qa.q: Where was Nadia during the call?
qa.a: In Kuala Lumpur.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling when she heard Nadia's long "Hmmm"?
qa.a: She felt anxious that it meant disapproval, and a little disappointed, since she had hoped Nadia would just say yes.

qa.q: What made the conversation useful for Mei?
qa.a: She asked what the hmm meant, and Nadia's honest question helped her see her real reason and write two lists.

qa.q: How did Nadia see her own "hmm"?
qa.a: Nadia saw it as thinking with a slight worry, not a flat no, and wanted Mei to check her reasons.

grounding: Shows a young adult hearing mm-hmm as following and a long hmm as doubt or thinking, and checking the meaning instead of assuming.

passage: On her first week as a trainee in the medical records department at the district hospital, Tanuja presented her idea for colour-coding patient files. Her supervisor, Manjula, listened with her pen tapping the desk. "Mm-hmm... mm-hmm." Then Tanuja got to the part about re-labelling the old files. Manjula went quiet and said, "Hmm." Just that. Tanuja's heart sank. She was sure it meant no. She almost said, "It's okay, forget it." Instead she asked, "Ma'am, is that a no-hmm or a thinking-hmm?" Manjula laughed. "A counting-hmm. There are about forty thousand old files. I was working out how long that would take. The idea's good for new files. Let's start there." Tanuja wrote it down, grinning. She realised she had nearly dropped a good idea over one syllable.

qa.q: How many old files does Manjula estimate there are?
qa.a: About forty thousand.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when Manjula said "Hmm"?
qa.a: Her heart sank and she felt discouraged, sure it meant no; she nearly gave up the idea.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do well when she heard the hmm?
qa.a: Instead of dropping the idea, she asked directly whether it was a no or a thinking hmm.

qa.q: What was Manjula actually doing when she said "Hmm"?
qa.a: She was working out how long re-labelling forty thousand old files would take, so it was a counting, thinking sound, not disagreement.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a supervisor's hmm as disagreement and checking to find it meant thinking.
